_about: Hand-built subset of the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, summarized in our own words (the criteria are copyrighted; never paste table text here). Owner: B. Entries checked against the paper on 2026-10-28 (see docs/DATA_SOURCES.md, verification log). Drug names are lower-case RxNorm ingredient names. Tags are subsets of the paper's classes, not the full lists.

source.title: American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults

drugs.label: Older-style (first-generation) antihistamines taken by mouth, often in night-time sleep aids
drugs.risk: Strongly anticholinergic: can cause confusion, dry mouth, constipation and falls; the body gets used to them as a sleep aid.
drugs.advice: Ask about a non-drowsy allergy medicine or other ways to improve sleep.

drugs.label: Benzodiazepines (anxiety or sleep medicines)
drugs.risk: Raise the risk of memory problems, confusion, falls, broken bones and car crashes. The body can become dependent on them.
drugs.advice: Ask about a plan to lower or replace it.

drugs.label: Z-drug sleeping pills
drugs.risk: Similar risks to benzodiazepines (confusion, falls, fractures) with little extra sleep.
drugs.advice: Ask about other ways to improve sleep.

drugs.label: Common anti-inflammatory pain relievers (NSAIDs) used regularly
drugs.risk: Regular use raises the risk of stomach bleeding and ulcers and can strain the kidneys.
drugs.advice: Avoid regular use unless other options do not work; ask about stomach protection.

drugs.label: Daily aspirin taken to prevent a first heart attack or stroke
drugs.risk: For people without heart disease, the bleeding risk can outweigh the benefit when started at an older age.
drugs.advice: If you take aspirin daily, ask whether you still need it.

drugs.label: Sulfonylurea diabetes pills used as a first or second choice
drugs.risk: Can cause dangerously low blood sugar and are linked to more heart problems and deaths than some other diabetes medicines.
drugs.advice: If this is one of your first diabetes medicines, ask whether a medicine with lower low-blood-sugar risk fits you.

drugs.label: Muscle relaxants
drugs.risk: Cause drowsiness and anticholinergic effects and raise fall risk; benefit at safe doses is doubtful.
drugs.advice: Ask about other options for muscle pain.

drugs.label: Stomach-acid reducers (proton pump inhibitors) taken every day for more than 8 weeks
drugs.risk: Long-term use is linked to gut infections, bone loss and fractures. Some people still need it, for example those at high risk of stomach bleeding (such as from regular NSAID or steroid use) or with certain conditions like erosive esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus.
drugs.advice: If you have taken it every day for more than 8 weeks, ask whether you still need it.

drugs.label: Warfarin started as the first blood thinner for atrial fibrillation or a blood clot
drugs.risk: When starting treatment, it has a higher bleeding risk than newer blood thinners for many people. It can still be the right choice when newer blood thinners cannot be used or are hard to get, and people who have taken it for a long time with steady results may reasonably stay on it.
drugs.advice: Do not stop it on your own; if you are just starting, ask whether a newer option suits you, unless newer options cannot be used or there are real barriers to them.

drugs.label: Older antidepressants and paroxetine
drugs.risk: Strongly anticholinergic and sedating, and can make you dizzy or faint when you stand up.

drugs.label: Metoclopramide (nausea / stomach emptying)
drugs.risk: Can cause movement problems, some of which may not go away. It can still be used for slow stomach emptying (gastroparesis), for no more than 12 weeks except in rare cases.
drugs.advice: Unless it is a short course for gastroparesis, ask whether you still need it.

drugs.label: Meperidine (opioid pain reliever)
drugs.risk: Works poorly at usual doses by mouth and is more likely than other opioids to cause confusion (delirium).
drugs.advice: Ask about a safer pain reliever.

drugs.label: Megestrol (appetite stimulant)
drugs.risk: Raises the risk of blood clots and possibly death, with little benefit for weight.
drugs.advice: Ask whether you still need it.

drugs.label: Mineral oil taken by mouth (laxative)
drugs.risk: Can be breathed into the lungs by accident.

combos.label: Two or more anticholinergic medicines
combos.risk: Effects add up and raise the risk of memory problems, confusion and falls.
combos.advice: Ask whether one of them can be stopped or replaced.

combos.label: Three or more medicines that act on the brain
combos.risk: Together they raise the risk of falls and broken bones.
combos.advice: Ask for a review of which ones are still needed.

combos.label: Opioid pain reliever + benzodiazepine
combos.risk: Together they can slow breathing and raise overdose risk.
combos.advice: Talk to your doctor soon about this combination.

combos.label: Opioid pain reliever + gabapentin or pregabalin
combos.risk: Together they can cause heavy sleepiness and slowed breathing. There are exceptions while switching from an opioid to gabapentin or pregabalin, or when gabapentin or pregabalin is used to lower the opioid dose, but caution is still needed.
combos.advice: Ask whether this combination is still needed.

combos.label: Warfarin + certain antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim)
combos.risk: Together they raise the risk of bleeding.
combos.advice: Avoid this combination when possible. If you need both, your blood-thinning test (INR) should be checked closely.
